newsitem.title: USA: New hearing set for Mexican immigrant in cop death.
newsitem.headline: New hearing set for Mexican immigrant in cop death.

text.p: A Texas judge on Thursday ordered a new hearing to determine if evidence used to convict a Mexican immigrant in the 1982 shooting of a Houston policeman was false.

Judge Frank Maloney said he would hear testimony starting on Feb. 17 before deciding whether to grant a defence motion to throw out the allegedly tainted evidence that resulted in Ricardo Aldape Guerra being sentenced to death.
Aldape was on Death Row for nearly 14 years before his conviction in state court was overturned by federal courts and a new trial ordered. He is currently in Harris County Jail.
"I want this thing to be terminated as soon as possible. This case is much too old and too many people have suffered," Maloney said.

Aldape was given the death sentence for allegedly killing police officer James Harris during a 1982 traffic stop. He said from the beginning that Harris was shot not by him, but by Roberto Carrasco Flores, who died in a shootout with police.

In 1994, U.S. District Judge Kenneth Hoyt threw out the conviction and ordered a new trial because he said police and prosecutors had manipulated evidence and intimidated witnesses to point the finger at Aldape. In a blistering attack, he said law enforcement officials had become "merchants of chaos."
Hoyt's ruling was affirmed last August by the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans, and Aldape, 34, was taken off Death Row at a prison in Huntsville, Texas.
The case was to be retried starting Dec. 2, but was postponed because of lack of courthouse space.
Defence attorney Scott Atlas said he hoped that if the judge agrees, the prosecutors will drop the case and Aldape can be freed immediately.
Maloney said it was possible a new trial could take place before this summer, but it could be delayed if either side appeals his ruling following the Feb. 17 hearings.

Prosecutor Casey O'Brien told reporters he would put on as many as 20 witnesses to dispute Hoyt's ruling that the original evidence was tainted. He also said the state was seeking DNA evidence to link Aldape to the crime.
Defence attorney Scott Atlas told reporters that Aldape, who came from the United States illegally in 1982 to find work, was anxious to return home to Monterrey, Mexico.

"The most important thing is for him to obtain his freedom while his parents are alive. Except for a few minutes in federal court in 1993...he has not been able to touch his parents or any member of his family since 1982," Atlas said.
